evidence: src/infrastructure/OrderController.ts updateOrderState: `if (!state || !['paid', 'packed', 'shipped', 'delivered'].includes(state))` hardcodes the allowed target states and leaves out 'placed'. This is an order-transition business rule that belongs in the domain layer.
src/infrastructure/OrderController.ts listOrdersByState: `!['placed', 'paid', 'packed', 'shipped', 'delivered'].includes(state)` repeats the domain's OrderState values inside the controller.
Everything else is transport work that fits the infrastructure layer: reading Express req/res, `res.status(201).json(response)`, and mapping errors to 400 responses.
parsedVerdict.reasoning:
OrderController sits in the infrastructure layer and mostly acts as an HTTP adapter. It reads Express request params, body and query, calls the injected use cases, maps results to status codes and JSON, and turns errors into 400 responses. All of that fits the infrastructure (transport) role.

The problem is in updateOrderState. It hardcodes which states an order may move to: ['paid', 'packed', 'shipped', 'delivered']. That list deliberately leaves out 'placed', which is a valid state, as listOrdersByState shows. Deciding which states an order can transition into is a business rule. It belongs in the domain layer (the Order entity or OrderState), or in the application use case, not in the transport layer.

listOrdersByState also hardcodes its own copy of the full state list instead of relying on the domain's definition. On its own that is closer to input parsing than a misplaced rule, but it spreads domain knowledge into the controller.

Confidence is moderate because some reviewers would treat the whitelist as plain request validation.

listOrdersByState repeats the domain's set of valid OrderState values as a hardcoded list (['placed','paid','packed','shipped','delivered']). That spreads domain knowledge into the infrastructure controller instead of using the domain layer's definition.
